import numpy as np

S=np.sign(X)
D=W@X
A=D-S
alpha=1.0
E=np.zeros((3,3)); E[0,0]=1
print('Example: n=r=3, k=2, h(Y)=||Y||_1, f(Y)=<A,Y>, H=Q=0, alpha=1')
print('X=',X.tolist())
print('A=',A.tolist())
print('Orthogonality error=',np.linalg.norm(X.T@X-np.eye(3)))
print('Full critical residual squared minimum over subgradient scalar u is 16*c"'^2 ='"',16*c*c)

strengths: The problem is relevant to sparse learning and matrix optimization. Extending orthogonal row updates to rectangular Stiefel matrices with separable nonsmooth regularizers is potentially useful.

The update preserves orthogonality, and the majorization construction provides a clear sufficient-descent mechanism. For two-row blocks, reducing optimization to rotations and reflections is computationally attractive.
Experiments cover ten datasets and three PCA formulations, with favorable reported objective values and nearly exact feasibility for nonnegative PCA.
weaknesses: The central stationarity claim is false under the stated assumptions. In Theorem 3.8(a), Eq. (38) allows a different subgradient for each block, whereas Eq. (39) requires one common subgradient. A concrete counterexample uses s=1/√2, X=[[0,s,s],[s,1/2,-1/2],[s,-1/2,1/2]], W=(1/4)[[0,1,-1],[-1,0,0],[1,0,0]], and F(Y)=⟨WX−S,Y⟩+||Y||₁, where S₁₁=0 and other entries equal sign(X). With Q=0 and α=1, identity globally minimizes every two-row surrogate at X, yet the minimum squared criticality residual ||G−XGᵀX||² is 1. Thus global block-2 stationarity need not imply criticality, also contradicting Lemma 4.4(b) and the general critical-point convergence claim.

The convergence analysis has an independent probabilistic error. In Appendix F.2, Eq. (51) is applied to a matrix depending on X^{t+1}, which itself depends on B^t. Equal marginal distributions of B^t and B^{t+1} do not justify exchanging these blocks inside that expectation. Appendix F.4 additionally treats bounds in expectation as pointwise bounds and removes a random objective-gap factor from an expectation. Consequently, the claimed KL finite-length and last-iterate rates are not established.

The main ℓ0-SPCA evaluation uses an essentially trivial optimization regime. Appendix G.2 normalizes ||A||F=1, so C=AᵀA has trace 1 and 0≤tr(XᵀCX)≤1. Every tested λ is at least 10; consequently, adding even one nonzero beyond the minimum r costs more than any possible variance improvement. The global solution therefore consists of signed coordinate vectors selecting the r largest diagonal entries of C. This exact sorting baseline is absent, and these experiments do not establish performance on meaningful sparsity–variance tradeoffs.

The exact subproblem solver is incorrect as described in Appendix B. The breakpoint satisfying xᵢ+t yᵢ=0 is −xᵢ/yᵢ, whereas the manuscript lists +xᵢ/yᵢ. Its instruction to discard coordinates with yᵢ=0 is also invalid for the ℓ1 case: λ|xᵢ|/√(1+t²) remains dependent on t. These details require correction because the strongest guarantees assume globally exact subproblem solutions.

Experimental controls and reporting are insufficient. For ℓ1-SPCA and nonnegative PCA, OBCD uses identity initialization while competitors use random initialization, confounding algorithmic improvements with initialization. There are no reported repeated-run uncertainties or substantive ablations of reflections, block size, or the proximal parameter. Baseline tuning is insufficiently documented, and the main text specifies 30-second comparisons while Table 1 specifies 40 seconds.

import math, itertools
s=1/math.sqrt(2)
X=[[0,s,s],[s,.5,-.5],[s,-.5,.5]]
D=[[0,-s/2,s/2],[s/2,0,0],[-s/2,0,0]]
def transpose(A):return list(map(list,zip(*A)))
def mul(A,B):return [[sum(a*b for a,b in zip(row,col)) for col in zip(*B)] for row in A]
S=[[0 if v==0 else (1 if v>0 else -1) for v in row] for row in X]
G0=[[v/2 for v in row] for row in mul(D,X)]
A=[[g-v for g,v in zip(gr,sr)] for gr,sr in zip(G0,S)]
def obj(Y):return sum(A[i][j]*Y[i][j]+abs(Y[i][j]) for i in range(3) for j in range(3))
print('X =',X)
print('linear gradient A =',A)
print('orthogonality error =',max(abs(v-(i==j)) for i,row in enumerate(mul(X,transpose(X))) for j,v in enumerate(row)))
print('full residual squared = 2*u"'^2 + 0.5 for u in [-1,1], minimum 0.5'"')
for (i,j),u in zip(itertools.combinations(range(3),2),[.5,-.5,0]):
    G=[r[:] for r in G0];G[0][0]+=u
    M=mul(G,transpose(X))
    sub=[[M[p][q] for q in [i,j]] for p in [i,j]]
    eigmax=(sub[0][0]+sub[1][1])/2+math.sqrt(((sub[0][0]-sub[1][1])/2)**2+sub[0][1]**2)
    best=(float('inf'),None)
    for det in [1,-1]:
        for z in range(8192):
            th=2*math.pi*z/8192;c=math.cos(th);t=math.sin(th)
            V=[[det*c,t],[-det*t,c]]
            Y=[r[:] for r in X]

            Y[j]=[V[1][0]*a+V[1][1]*b for a,b in zip(X[i],X[j])]

            gap=obj(Y)-obj(X)+penalty
            if gap<best[0]:best=(gap,(det,th))
    print('block', (i+1,j+1),'subgradient u =',u,'M_B =',sub,'max eigenvalue =',eigmax,'minimum sampled surrogate gap =',best)

strengths: The row-block update preserves orthogonality exactly and offers inexpensive iterations for rectangular Stiefel problems.
The majorization construction supports a useful sufficient-decrease guarantee under exact subproblem minimization. Reducing two-row updates to rotations and reflections is practically appealing.
Experiments cover ten datasets and three PCA formulations, with several relevant recent baselines and reported objective and feasibility measurements.
weaknesses: The central stationarity hierarchy, Theorem 3.8(a), is false under the stated assumptions. Equation (38) establishes a potentially different subgradient G_B for each block, whereas Lemma A.1 requires one common G. A counterexample uses s=1/sqrt(2), X=[[0,s,s],[s,1/2,-1/2],[s,-1/2,1/2]], D=(s/2)[[0,-1,1],[1,0,0],[-1,0,0]], h(Y)=||Y||_1 and f(Y)=<DX/2-S,Y>, where S is the entrywise sign of X with S_11=0. With Q=0 and alpha=1, every two-row surrogate satisfies K(V)-K(I_2) >= (1-s/4)||V-I_2||_F^2/2, so X is BS2. Nevertheless, its squared stationarity residual under Definition 3.4 is 1/2. Thus OBCD can remain at a noncritical point, also contradicting Lemma 4.4(b) and Theorem 4.6.

The convergence analysis has additional substantive gaps. Equations (51)-(52) interchange the previously selected block and a fresh independent block when evaluating a matrix depending on X^{t+1}; that matrix depends on the previous block, invalidating the interchange. Appendix F.4 subsequently uses expectation bounds as pointwise bounds inside correlated random products. It also substitutes the global infimum F_infinity for the limiting objective value without establishing global optimality. The claimed KL and last-iterate guarantees are consequently unsupported.

The claimed exact subproblem solver contains consequential errors. Appendix B lists t=x_i/y_i as a zero of x_i+t*y_i, whereas the correct breakpoint is -x_i/y_i. It also discards entries with y_i=0, although their L1 contribution |x_i|/sqrt(1+t^2) generally changes the minimizer. These errors require correction and validation because exact minimization underpins the guarantees.

The main L0 experiments use a degenerate regularization regime. Appendix G.2 normalizes ||A||_F=1, giving trace(C)=1 and 0 <= trace(X^T C X) <= 1. All tested penalties satisfy lambda>1, so every global optimum has exactly r nonzeros: any additional nonzero costs more than the entire possible variance gain. The exact solution therefore selects the r coordinate axes with largest C_ii. This elementary exact baseline is missing, and the experiments do not establish performance on meaningful sparsity–variance tradeoffs.

Experimental controls are insufficient to attribute improvements to the method. All L1 baselines use random initialization while OBCD uses identity initialization. Repeated-run uncertainty and ablations isolating reflections, proximal regularization, and block size are absent. Runtime reporting is inconsistent: the main text specifies 30 seconds while Table 1 specifies 40 seconds. These limitations further weaken the broad superiority claims.

strengths: The row-wise orthogonal update preserves feasibility exactly and permits partial-gradient computation, avoiding repeated full-matrix retractions.
Reducing two-row updates to scalar optimization over rotations and reflections is a useful construction for handling separable nonsmooth penalties.
The manuscript provides extensive algorithmic detail and experiments across three PCA formulations and ten datasets. The reported nonnegative-PCA improvements are promising.
weaknesses: The central stationarity hierarchy is false as stated. Appendix E.3 moves from a potentially different subgradient for each block in Eq. (38) to one common subgradient in Eq. (39). A concrete counterexample uses n=r=3, k=2, alpha=1, H=Q=0, and F(Y)=<A,Y>+||Y||_1, with X=[[0.6,0.8,0],[-0.48,0.36,0.8],[0.64,-0.48,0.6]] and A=[[-0.808,-1.144,-0.07],[1.12,-0.84,-1],[-1.09,0.88,-1]]. Here X is orthogonal and the identity is the unique global minimizer of every two-row surrogate, but the minimum squared stationarity residual from Definition 3.4 is 0.4608. Thus OBCD remains at a noncritical point. This directly contradicts Theorem 3.8(a), Lemma 4.4(b), and the critical-point complexity guarantee.

The convergence proofs contain additional substantive gaps. In Appendix F.2, Eq. (52), step 2 replaces the selected block with a fresh random block even though the matrix being restricted depends on the iterate produced using the selected block. Equal marginal sampling distributions do not justify this exchange. Appendix F.4 also applies the KL inequality using the global infimum F_infinity rather than the limiting objective value, without establishing global optimality. The claimed last-iterate rates therefore lack a valid justification.

The main sparse-PCA evaluation is degenerate under the reported scaling. Appendix G.2 normalizes ||A||_F=1, so C=A^T A has trace 1 and 0<=tr(X^T C X)<=1. With every tested lambda>=10, an additional nonzero costs more than any possible variance improvement. Consequently, the global solution of the reported l0 problem has exactly r nonzeros and is obtained simply by selecting the r largest diagonal entries of C. This exact sorting baseline is missing, and these experiments do not demonstrate performance on nontrivial sparse-loading problems.

The experimental comparisons do not adequately isolate algorithmic advantages. For l1 sparse PCA, OBCD receives identity initialization while all competitors receive random initialization. No repeated-run uncertainty estimates or initialization ablations are reported. Claims that competitors remain trapped regardless of runtime are also unsupported by the finite runtime plots.

The exact subproblem solver needs corrections. Appendix B lists x_i/y_i as the breakpoint solving x_i+t*y_i=0, whereas the correct value is -x_i/y_i. It also proposes dropping coordinates with y_i=0, although their l1 contribution |x_i|/sqrt(1+t^2) generally affects the minimizer. These errors undermine reproducibility of the global-solution procedure as written; efficient exact nonsmooth optimization for general k additionally remains an assumption.

The majorization construction provides a sound sufficient-decrease mechanism. Considering both rotations and reflections covers both components of O(2).
The manuscript provides extensive derivations and experiments across ten datasets and three PCA formulations, including comparisons with ManPG, RADMM, and RSSM.
weaknesses: The central stationarity claim, Theorem 3.8(a), is false under the stated assumptions. Equation (38) allows a different subgradient for each block, whereas Equation (39) requires one subgradient satisfying every block simultaneously. A concrete counterexample uses q=1/√2, X0=[[0,q,q],[q,1/2,-1/2],[q,-1/2,1/2]], A=[[0,1,-1],[-1,0,0],[1,0,0]]/4, and F(Y)=⟨AX0−S,Y⟩+||Y||1, where S is the entrywise sign of X0 with S11=0. Every two-row orthogonal update has objective at least F(X0), so X0 is BS2 for H=0 and any α>0. Nevertheless, min over G∈∂F(X0) of ||G−X0GᵀX0||F equals 1. Thus OBCD can remain at a noncritical point, also contradicting Lemma 4.4(b) and Theorem 4.6.

The stochastic convergence proofs contain additional substantial gaps. Equation (52) exchanges the previously selected block with a fresh block even though X^{t+1} depends on the previous selection; equal marginal sampling distributions do not justify this exchange. Appendix F.4 also takes random objective-gap terms outside conditional expectations and substitutes the global infimum for the limiting objective value without justification. The claimed KL finite-length and last-iterate guarantees are therefore not established.

The exact subproblem solver is incorrect as written. Appendix B lists x_i/y_i as a breakpoint of x_i+t y_i=0, whereas the breakpoint is −x_i/y_i. It also permits discarding coordinates with y_i=0; for the ℓ1 objective, these contribute the nonconstant term λ|x_i|/√(1+t²). These errors require correction and validation because exact global subproblem solutions underpin the guarantees.

The main ℓ0 sparse-PCA experiments use a mathematically trivial global-optimization regime. Appendix G.2 normalizes ||A||F=1, implying tr(C)=1 and 0≤tr(XᵀCX)≤1. With every tested λ≥10, any solution having more than r nonzeros is worse than a signed coordinate frame: λ(r+1)−1>λr. Consequently, the global optimum simply selects the r largest diagonal entries of C. This direct sorting baseline is missing, and the results do not establish performance on a substantive sparsity–variance tradeoff.

The ℓ1 comparisons confound algorithm quality with initialization: OBCD starts from an identity frame, while every comparator starts randomly. This particularly favors OBCD under the very large sparsity penalties used. Matched initializations, repeated trials with uncertainty estimates, and ablations isolating reflections and surrogate choices are needed to support the broad superiority claims.

strengths: The rowwise orthogonal update preserves feasibility exactly and supports partial or incremental gradient computation, offering a useful approach to reducing per-iteration costs.

The rotation/reflection formulation provides a promising way to handle nonsmooth penalties through small subproblems. The basic sufficient-decrease argument is convincing under the exact-solution assumption.
Experiments cover ten datasets and three PCA variants, include relevant baselines such as ManPG, RSSM, and RADMM, and report substantial objective improvements, particularly for nonnegative PCA.
weaknesses: The central stationarity claim is false under the stated assumptions. Appendix E.3, equations (38)–(39), incorrectly replaces a potentially different subgradient for each block with one common subgradient. An explicit counterexample has n=3, r=k=2, q=1/sqrt(2), X=[[0,q],[q,1/2],[q,-1/2]], h(Y)=||Y||_1, and f(Y)=-Y12-Y21-Y31-(3/2)Y22+(3/2)Y32. Every two-row orthogonal update satisfies F(Y)>=F(X), making X a BS2 point for H=Q=0 and any positive proximal parameter. However, its subgradients are G=[[s,0],[0,-1/2],[0,1/2]], with |s|<=1, and min_G ||G-XG^T X||_F^2=1/4. Thus OBCD can remain at a noncritical point. This contradicts Theorem 3.8(a), Lemma 4.4(b), and the critical-point convergence claim in Theorem 4.6.

The stochastic convergence proofs contain additional substantive gaps. In Appendix F.2, equations (51)–(52), an averaging identity for a fixed matrix is applied to a matrix depending on X^{t+1}, although X^{t+1} depends on the sampled block B^t. Appendix F.4 also uses expectation bounds as pointwise inequalities and moves a random objective decrement outside the expectation. The claimed KL finite-length and last-iterate guarantees are therefore not established.

The exact subproblem solver is incorrect as written. Appendix B uses t=x_i/y_i as a breakpoint for x_i+t*y_i=0, whereas the breakpoint is -x_i/y_i. Its instruction to discard terms with y_i=0 is also invalid for the ℓ1 penalty: the contribution |x_i|/sqrt(1+t^2) still depends on t. These errors require correction and implementation validation because the theoretical guarantees assume globally solved subproblems.

The main ℓ0 experiments occupy a trivial optimization regime under the stated normalization. Appendix G.2 sets ||A||_F=1, implying trace(C)=1 and 0<=trace(X^T C X)<=1. Since every tested regularization weight exceeds 1, a global minimizer must have exactly r nonzeros and can be obtained simply by selecting the r largest diagonal entries of C. This exact baseline is omitted, and the experiments do not establish effectiveness in nontrivial sparse-PCA regimes.

The empirical comparisons have important confounds. For ℓ1 and nonnegative PCA, OBCD uses identity initialization while competitors use random initialization, without matched-initialization ablations. Repeated-run variability, baseline tuning, and ablations isolating reflection updates are not adequately reported. Runtime budgets are also inconsistent: the main text specifies 30 seconds, Table 1 specifies 40 seconds, and the associated curves extend to 60 seconds.

strengths: The row-wise orthogonal update preserves orthogonality exactly and supports a useful sufficient-descent inequality with partial-gradient computations.
Reducing two-row subproblems to searches over rotations and reflections is a useful algorithmic idea for separable nonsmooth optimization.
Experiments cover ten datasets and three PCA formulations, include relevant baselines, and report promising nonnegative PCA results across four ranks.
weaknesses: The central stationarity hierarchy is false under the stated assumptions. Appendix E.3, equations (38)–(39), incorrectly replaces 'each block admits a suitable subgradient' with 'one subgradient satisfies every block.' A counterexample is q=1/sqrt(2), X=[[q,q,0],[-1/2,1/2,q],[1/2,-1/2,q]], h(Y)=||Y||_1, and f(Y)=<A,Y>, where A=[[-1-q/4,-1+q/4,0],[7/8,-9/8,-1],[-7/8,9/8,-1]]. With Q=0 and alpha=1, every two-row surrogate is uniquely minimized by I_2, yet the minimum of ||G-XG^T X||_F^2 over G in ∂F(X) is 1/2. Thus a BS2 point need not be critical, contradicting Theorem 3.8(a), Lemma 4.4(b), and the general critical-point convergence claim.

The convergence proofs contain additional substantive gaps. Equation (52) applies the sampling identity (51) to a quantity depending on X^{t+1}, although X^{t+1} depends on the previously selected block B^t; that block cannot be interchanged with an independent fresh block. The KL argument also removes random factors from conditional expectations without justification and substitutes the global infimum F∞ for the attained limiting objective value. Consequently, the advertised last-iterate guarantees are not established.

The exact subproblem solver is incorrect as written. Appendix B lists x_i/y_i as a breakpoint of x_i+t y_i=0, whose root is actually -x_i/y_i. It also says terms with y_i=0 can be removed without affecting the minimizer, although their ℓ1 contribution is lambda|x_i|/sqrt(1+t^2), which varies with t. These issues require correction and validation because exact global subproblem minimization underpins the method.

The ℓ0 experiments use a mathematically degenerate regularization regime. Appendix G.2 normalizes ||A||_F=1, implying 0≤tr(X^T A^T A X)≤1, while every tested lambda is at least 10. Since orthogonality requires at least r nonzeros, every global optimum must have exactly r nonzeros and can be obtained simply by selecting the r largest covariance diagonal entries. This exact baseline is missing, and these experiments do not establish performance on a meaningful sparsity–variance tradeoff.

The empirical comparisons do not adequately isolate the algorithm's contribution. For ℓ1 PCA, all baselines start randomly while OBCD starts at an identity matrix, which already minimizes the sparsity penalty. Matched initializations, repeated-run uncertainty, and application-level ablations of reflections and proximal parameters are absent. Timing descriptions also conflict: the prose specifies 30 seconds, Table 1 specifies 40, and Table 2 specifies 60. These limitations weaken the claims of consistent superiority.

strengths: The row-block update preserves orthogonality exactly and offers potentially inexpensive iterations for structured quadratic objectives.
The rotation/reflection parameterization provides a useful approach to two-row nonsmooth subproblems. The basic sufficient-decrease argument is sound under exact minimization.
Experiments cover ten datasets and three PCA formulations, include relevant optimization baselines, and report feasibility violations for nonnegative PCA.
weaknesses: The central stationarity claim is false under the stated assumptions. Consider F(Y)=<A,Y>+||Y||_1, q=1/sqrt(2), X=[[0,q],[q,1/2],[q,-1/2]], and A=[[0,-1],[-1,-1/2],[-1,1/2]], with k=2, H=Q=0, and alpha=1. For every block, K(V;X,B)-K(I;X,B)>=||V-I||_F^2/4, so X is a BS2 point and OBCD remains there. Nevertheless, dist^2(0,partial_M F(X))=1/4: X is not critical. This contradicts Theorem 3.8(a), Lemma 4.4(b), and Theorem 4.6. The underlying error in Appendix E.3 is exchanging 'for every block there exists a subgradient' with 'there exists one subgradient satisfying every block.'

The stochastic convergence analysis has additional substantive gaps. Equations (51)-(52) exchange the previous and next sampled blocks while the matrix being sampled depends on X^{t+1}, and therefore on the previous block. Identical sampling distributions do not justify this exchange. Appendix F.4 also takes random objective differences outside conditional expectations and uses the global infimum F_infinity where the KL argument requires the attained limiting objective value. The claimed KL convergence rates are consequently unestablished.

The main L0-PCA benchmark is degenerate. Appendix G.2 normalizes ||A||_F=1, implying tr(C)=1 and 0<=tr(X^T C X)<=1. Every tested lambda exceeds 1. Any feasible point with at least r+1 nonzeros therefore has objective at least lambda(r+1)-1>lambda*r, whereas an r-coordinate frame has objective at most lambda*r. Thus the global optimum has exactly r nonzeros and is obtained simply by selecting the r largest diagonal entries of C. This exact baseline is missing, and the experiments do not establish performance in meaningful variance-versus-sparsity regimes.

The L1 comparison confounds algorithm quality with initialization: OBCD starts from a sparse identity matrix, while every competitor starts randomly. This particularly favors OBCD under the enormous regularization penalties used. There are no reported multi-seed uncertainty estimates or controlled ablations of initialization, reflections, block size, or proximal strength. Finite runtime curves also cannot establish the claim that competitors remain trapped regardless of how long they run.

The exact-subproblem solver specification contains material errors. Appendix B gives x_i/y_i as the breakpoint for x_i+t*y_i=0, whereas it should be -x_i/y_i. It also discards entries with y_i=0, although their L1 contribution lambda*|x_i|/sqrt(1+t^2) still depends on t. These require correction and verification because exact global subproblem minimization underpins the proposed guarantees.

strengths: The row-wise orthogonal update is a useful, feasibility-preserving construction that accommodates rectangular Stiefel manifolds and separable nonsmooth objectives.

The basic majorization and sufficient-descent argument is sound under exact subproblem minimization. Reducing two-row updates to one-dimensional rotation/reflection searches is computationally appealing.
Experiments cover three PCA formulations, ten datasets, and relevant baselines. The reported nonnegative-PCA results show substantial objective improvements with negligible nonnegativity violations.
weaknesses: The central stationarity claim, Theorem 3.8(a), is false under the stated assumptions. Appendix E.3 incorrectly replaces a potentially different subgradient for each block with one subgradient satisfying every block condition. A concrete counterexample uses s=1/sqrt(2), X=[[0,s,s],[s,-1/2,1/2],[s,1/2,-1/2]], h(Y)=||Y||_1, and f(Y)=<M,Y>, where M=[[0,s/4-1,-s/4-1],[-1,9/8,-7/8],[-1,-9/8,7/8]]. With H=Q=0 and alpha=1, every two-row surrogate is globally minimized at I_2, but min over G in ∂F(X) of ||G-XG^T X||_F^2 equals 1/2. Thus OBCD can remain indefinitely at a noncritical point. This also contradicts Lemma 4.4(b) and Theorem 4.6.

The main ℓ0 experiments reduce to a simple feature-selection problem. Appendix G.2 normalizes ||A||_F=1, so C=A^T A has trace 1 and 0≤tr(X^T C X)≤1. With every tested lambda≥10, any solution with more than r nonzeros is worse than a signed coordinate basis. Consequently, a global optimum follows simply by selecting the r largest diagonal entries of C. This exact baseline is absent, and the experiments do not demonstrate performance in a meaningful sparsity–variance tradeoff regime.

The randomized convergence proofs contain additional substantive gaps. Equation (52) exchanges the updated block with a fresh random block although X^(t+1) depends on the updated block, invalidating the use of Equation (51). Appendix F.4 also uses expectation bounds as pointwise bounds inside random products and substitutes the global infimum F∞ for the limiting objective value required by the KL inequality. The claimed last-iterate guarantees are therefore not established.

The exact subproblem solver derivation contains correctness errors. Appendix B lists x_i/y_i as a root of x_i+t y_i=0, where the root should be -x_i/y_i. It also discards coordinates with y_i=0, although their ℓ1 contribution lambda|x_i|/sqrt(1+t^2) generally depends on t. These errors undermine the stated exact-solve justification, particularly for sparse initializations.

The comparisons do not adequately isolate algorithmic benefits. In the ℓ1 experiments, OBCD receives identity initialization while all baselines receive random initialization. There are no reported repeated-run uncertainties or ablations isolating reflections, block size, or the proximal parameter. Timing is also inconsistent: the main text specifies 30 seconds while Table 1 specifies 40 seconds. These limitations weaken the broad claims of consistently superior efficiency and solution quality.

strengths: The row-update scheme preserves orthogonality exactly, uses partial gradients, and admits a sound sufficient-descent argument under exact subproblem minimization.
Reducing two-row subproblems to rotations and reflections provides a useful approach to handling nonsmooth penalties without full-matrix retractions.
Experiments cover ten real or synthetic datasets and three PCA formulations, with extensive convergence plots and generally favorable reported objective values.
weaknesses: The central optimality hierarchy, Theorem 3.8(a), is false under the stated assumptions. Equation (38) provides a potentially different subgradient for each block, whereas Equation (39) requires one common subgradient. A concrete counterexample uses n=r=3, a=1/sqrt(2), X=[[0,a,a],[a,1/2,-1/2],[a,-1/2,1/2]], h(Y)=||Y||_1, and f(Y)=<L,Y>, where L=[[0,-1+a/4,-1-a/4],[-1,-9/8,7/8],[-1,9/8,-7/8]]. With H=Q=0 and alpha=1, every two-row surrogate is globally minimized at I_2, but the squared full stationarity residual is 1/2. Thus X is block-2 stationary without being critical. This also contradicts Lemma 4.4(b) and the critical-point guarantee in Theorem 4.6.

The stochastic convergence proofs contain additional substantive errors. Equation (51) exchanges the updated block with a fresh random block, then applies this identity to a matrix depending on X^{t+1}, which itself depends on the updated block. Equal marginal sampling probabilities do not justify this exchange. Appendix F.4 subsequently uses expectation bounds as pointwise inequalities and removes dependent random factors from expectations. The claimed KL finite-length and last-iterate rates therefore remain unsupported.

The principal ℓ0 experiments are mathematically degenerate. Appendix G.2 normalizes ||A||_F=1, so C=A^T A has trace 1 and 0<=tr(X^T C X)<=1. With every tested lambda at least 10, an additional nonzero costs more than any possible variance improvement. Every global optimum therefore has exactly r nonzeros and is obtained by selecting the r largest diagonal entries of C. This elementary exact baseline is missing, and these experiments do not establish performance on a meaningful sparsity–variance tradeoff.

The advertised exact breakpoint solver has errors as written. Appendix B discards coordinates with y_i=0, although their ℓ1 contribution, lambda*|x_i|/sqrt(1+t^2), depends on t and must be retained. It also identifies zeros of x_i+t*y_i at t=x_i/y_i instead of -x_i/y_i. These issues require correction and verification before the exact-subproblem guarantee can support the algorithm.

The empirical comparisons do not adequately isolate algorithmic advantages. The ℓ1 and nonnegative PCA experiments initialize OBCD with an identity matrix while using random initialization for competitors. Matched-start comparisons, baseline tuning details, repeated-seed uncertainty, and ablations of reflections and exact minimization are absent. Timing descriptions are also inconsistent: the main text specifies 30 seconds, Table 1 specifies 40 seconds, and later tables specify 60 seconds.

A counterexample uses n=r=3, k=2, α=1, Q=0, h(Y)=||Y||₁, and f(Y)=⟨A,Y⟩, with X=[[0,0.6,0.8],[0.6,0.64,-0.48],[-0.8,0.48,-0.36]] and A=[[-0.07,-0.808,-1.144],[-1,-1.09,0.88],[1,-1.12,0.84]]. Here X is orthogonal and every block surrogate is globally minimized at I₂, yet min_{G∈∂F(X)}||G−XGᵀX||²_F=0.4608. Appendices F.4–F.5 also use expectation bounds as pointwise inequalities and replace the cluster-point objective F(X∞) with F∞, previously defined as the global infimum. strengths: The row updates preserve orthogonality exactly, support rectangular Stiefel matrices, and can exploit partial gradients to reduce iteration cost.
The two-row reduction to rotations and reflections provides a useful computational approach to nonsmooth objectives. The MM sufficient-decrease argument is a sound component.

Experiments cover ten data sources and three PCA formulations, with several relevant baselines. The nonnegative-PCA results report substantial objective improvements and very small feasibility violations.
weaknesses: The central claim that BS2 points are necessarily critical is false under the stated assumptions. Appendix E.3 moves from block-specific subgradients in (38) to a common subgradient in (39); Lemma 4.4(b) similarly interchanges subgradient minimization and block averaging. A concrete counterexample uses q=1/√2, X=[[0,q,q],[q,1/2,-1/2],[-q,1/2,-1/2]], h(Y)=||Y||₁, and f(Y)=⟨C,Y⟩ with C=[[0,-1-q/4,-1+q/4],[-1,-7/8,9/8],[1,-7/8,9/8]]. Set H=Q=0 and α=1. Choosing the subgradient entry at X11 separately as 1/2 and -1/2 satisfies the respective blocks {1,2} and {1,3}; block {2,3} is already stationary. The resulting block gradient matrices are symmetric with norms at most 1/4, so the convex subgradient inequality and proximal term make I₂ the global minimizer of every block surrogate. Nevertheless, the minimum full squared stationarity residual is min_{s∈[-1,1]}(1/2+2s²)=1/2. Thus OBCD can remain at a noncritical BS2 point, also contradicting Theorem 4.6.

There are independent convergence-proof errors. In Appendix F.2, (51) equates block averages for a fixed matrix, but (52) applies this identity to a matrix depending on X^{t+1}, which itself depends on the previously selected block. Resampling a fresh block does not preserve that expectation. The KL proof additionally substitutes F∞, defined as the global infimum, for the limiting objective value without proving global optimality, and uses expected bounds as pointwise bounds. These gaps undermine the advertised last-iterate guarantees.

The principal ℓ0 experiments are mathematically trivial under the stated scaling. Appendix G.2 normalizes ||A||F=1, so C=AᵀA has trace 1 and 0≤tr(XᵀCX)≤1. With every tested λ≥10, any feasible matrix having at least r+1 nonzeros has objective at least λ(r+1)-1>λr. Consequently, every global optimum has exactly r nonzeros and is obtained by selecting the r largest diagonal entries of C. This exact baseline is absent, and the experiments do not establish performance in a meaningful sparsity-versus-explained-variance regime.

The empirical comparisons do not isolate algorithmic advantages. For ℓ1 and nonnegative PCA, OBCD uses identity initialization while competitors use random initialization, which can materially affect nonconvex solution quality. Repeated-run uncertainty and baseline tuning are not adequately reported. The stated 30-second evaluation budget also conflicts with Table 1's 40-second budget. Claims that competitors necessarily remain trapped in inferior local minima exceed this evidence.

The practical nonsmooth contribution focuses on k=2; efficient global solution for general k is assumed rather than supplied. There are no convincing ablations isolating reflections, surrogate choice, proximal strength, or block size. Given the established Givens-coordinate and MM foundations, the invalid optimality claims and inadequate experimental controls leave the paper's claimed advance insufficiently supported.

strengths: The paper addresses an important optimization problem encompassing sparse PCA and nonnegative PCA.
Orthogonal row updates preserve feasibility exactly and permit partial-gradient computation. The majorization construction provides a useful sufficient-decrease mechanism.
The rotation/reflection parameterization offers a practical approach to two-row subproblems, and the experiments cover ten datasets and several relevant baselines.
weaknesses: The central optimality hierarchy is false under the stated assumptions. Equation (38) establishes a potentially different subgradient for each block, whereas Equation (39) requires one common subgradient. A counterexample uses a=1/sqrt(2), X=[[0,a,a],[a,1/2,-1/2],[-a,1/2,-1/2]], h(Y)=||Y||_1, and f(Y)=<M,Y>, where M=[[0,a/4-1,-a/4-1],[-1,-9/8,7/8],[1,-9/8,7/8]]. With H=Q=0 and alpha=1, every two-row surrogate is uniquely minimized at I_2: suitable block supporting matrices are symmetric with operator norm at most a/4, so the proximal term ensures global minimality. Nevertheless, min_{G in partial F(X)} ||G-XG^T X||_F^2=1/2. This contradicts Theorem 3.8(a) and Lemma 4.4(b); OBCD can remain at a noncritical point.

The convergence analysis contains additional substantive errors. Equation (52), step (ii), exchanges sampling over B^t and B^{t+1} for a residual depending on X^{t+1}, which itself depends on B^t. Identical marginal block distributions do not justify this exchange. Appendix F.4 subsequently treats expected residual bounds as pointwise inequalities and removes random objective differences from expectations. The claimed criticality complexity and KL convergence guarantees therefore lack valid proofs.

The main sparse-PCA benchmark is mathematically degenerate. Appendix G.2 normalizes ||A||_F=1, implying trace(C)=1 and 0<=trace(X^T C X)<=1. With every tested lambda at least 10, an additional nonzero costs more than the entire possible variance improvement. Every global solution of the stated l0 problem therefore has exactly r nonzeros and consists of signed coordinate vectors corresponding to the r largest diagonal entries of C. This exact solution requires only sorting, yet that baseline is absent. Table 1 consequently does not demonstrate effectiveness on challenging sparse-PCA instances.

The claimed exact subproblem solver is incorrect as written. Appendix B lists t=x_i/y_i as a breakpoint of x_i+t*y_i=0, although the correct value is -x_i/y_i. It also instructs readers to discard coordinates with y_i=0. For l1 regularization, these contribute lambda*|x_i|/sqrt(1+t^2), which is not constant; for nonnegativity constraints, discarding them can remove an infeasibility condition. These issues directly affect the global-solution oracle required by the theory.

The remaining empirical evidence has substantial confounds. All l1 and nonnegative-PCA baselines use random initialization, while OBCD uses sparse identity initialization. Matched initializations, repeated-run uncertainty, adequately documented baseline tuning, and dataset-level ablations isolating reflections and exact subproblem minimization are missing. Consequently, the reported gains cannot be reliably attributed to the proposed algorithmic contributions.

strengths: The row-block update preserves orthogonality exactly and permits partial-gradient computation, offering a useful design for nonsmooth optimization on the Stiefel manifold.
The majorization construction provides a straightforward sufficient-descent argument. Reducing two-row subproblems to one-dimensional searches over rotations and reflections is practically appealing.
Experiments cover L0/L1 sparse PCA and nonnegative PCA across ten datasets, include relevant optimization baselines, and report promising objective values.
weaknesses: The central stationarity claim is false under the stated assumptions. Theorem 3.8(a)'s proof incorrectly replaces a separately chosen subgradient for each block with one common subgradient. An explicit counterexample uses u=1/sqrt(2), X=[[0,u],[u,1/2],[u,-1/2]], f(Y)=<A,Y> with A=[[0,-1],[-1,-3/2],[-1,3/2]], h(Y)=||Y||_1, H=Q=0, and alpha=1. Subgradients at X are G_s=[[s,0],[0,-1/2],[0,1/2]], |s|<=1. Blocks {1,2} and {1,3} require s=-1/2 and s=1/2, respectively, while block {2,3} is stationary for every s. Each block's supporting linear matrix has largest eigenvalue at most 1/4, so the proximal term makes I_2 its global surrogate minimizer. Nevertheless, min_s ||G_s-X G_s^T X||_F^2=1/4. Thus X is globally block-2 stationary but not critical, and OBCD initialized there never moves. This also contradicts Lemma 4.4(b) and Theorem 4.6.

The stochastic and KL convergence proofs contain additional substantive gaps. In Appendix F.2, Eqs. (51)-(52) exchange the current and next sampled blocks for a matrix depending on X^{t+1}, which itself depends on the current block. Appendix F.4 then uses expected bounds as pointwise inequalities and extracts random objective differences from expectations. It also uses F_infinity, defined as the global infimum, where the attained limiting objective is required. Consequently, the claimed last-iterate rates are not established. The bounded-subgradient assumption additionally excludes the principal L0 and nonnegativity-indicator applications.

The exact subproblem solver is incorrect as written. Appendix B gives L0 zero-crossing candidates as x_i/y_i, although x_i+t*y_i=0 requires -x_i/y_i. It also claims coordinates with y_i=0 can be discarded; for L1 regularization, their contribution |x_i|/sqrt(1+t^2) still depends on t. These errors require correction and validation because the principal guarantees assume globally exact subproblem solutions.

The main L0 experiments use a degenerate regularization regime. Appendix G.2 normalizes ||A||_F=1, implying trace(C)=1 and 0<=trace(X^T C X)<=1. Every tested lambda is at least 10, so one additional nonzero costs more than any possible variance improvement. Therefore every global optimum has exactly r nonzeros, and the stated problem is solved simply by selecting the r largest diagonal entries of C and their coordinate axes. This missing baseline substantially undermines the empirical contribution; the experiments do not demonstrate performance on meaningful sparse-PCA tradeoffs.

The comparisons lack important controls and reproducibility details. For L1 PCA and nonnegative PCA, OBCD uses identity initialization while competitors use random initialization. The manuscript does not specify baseline tuning or random seeds, report uncertainty across repeated runs, or provide ablations isolating reflections, surrogate choices, and block size. Section 5 states a 30-second evaluation budget while Table 1 specifies 40 seconds. More informative regularization ranges, matched initializations, specialized nonnegative-PCA baselines, and variance-versus-sparsity measurements are needed to substantiate the broad superiority claims.

Under exact surrogate minimization, the basic sufficient-decrease argument is sound. Parameterizing O(2) through rotations and reflections provides a promising route to tractable nonsmooth subproblems.
The experiments cover three relevant PCA formulations and ten datasets. Table 3 reports substantial objective improvements for nonnegative PCA with feasibility maintained to numerical precision.
weaknesses: The central stationarity hierarchy is false under the stated assumptions. Theorem 3.8(a) and Lemma 4.4(b) incorrectly replace block-dependent subgradient choices with one common subgradient (Eq. 38 and Eqs. 57–58). A counterexample uses n=r=3, k=2, Q=0, alpha=1, h(Y)=||Y||_1, and s=1/sqrt(2). Set X=[[0,s,s],[s,1/2,-1/2],[-s,1/2,-1/2]] and f(Y)=<A,Y>, where A=[[0,s/4-1,-s/4-1],[-1,-9/8,7/8],[1,-9/8,7/8]]. Identity globally minimizes every block surrogate, yet the squared criticality residual in Definition 3.4 equals 1/2. Thus OBCD can remain at a BS2 point that is not critical, contradicting a main contribution and the claimed critical-point convergence.

The stochastic and KL convergence proofs contain additional substantive gaps. Equation 51 is applied to a matrix depending on X^{t+1}, which depends on the selected block B^t; identical sampling distributions do not justify exchanging B^t with the independent next block. Appendix F.4 subsequently applies expectation bounds inside products and extracts random objective differences without justification. It also substitutes the globally defined F_infinity for the limit-point objective in the KL inequality without establishing equality. The last-iterate guarantees therefore remain unsupported.

The exact subproblem solver is incorrect as written. Appendix B lists x_i/y_i as a zero of x_i+t*y_i, whereas the breakpoint is -x_i/y_i. It also permits deleting terms with y_i=0, although their L1 contribution, lambda*|x_i|/sqrt(1+t^2), is generally nonconstant. These errors matter because exact global subproblem solutions underpin the algorithm's strongest guarantees.

The headline L0 experiments use a regime with a simple global solution. Appendix G.2 normalizes ||A||_F=1, so C=A^T A has trace 1 and the variance term lies between 0 and 1. Every tested lambda is at least 10; consequently, any feasible matrix with more than r nonzeros is worse than a coordinate solution with exactly r nonzeros. Global optimization therefore reduces to selecting the r largest diagonal entries of C. This exact baseline is missing, and these experiments do not establish performance on substantive sparse-PCA tradeoffs.

Experimental comparisons do not adequately isolate algorithmic benefits. For L1 and nonnegative PCA, OBCD uses identity initialization while competitors use random initialization. Repeated-run uncertainty, baseline parameter tuning, and ablations of reflections, block size, and surrogate choice are not reported. The stated 30-second budget also conflicts with the 40-second budget in Table 1. Matched initializations, meaningful regularization ranges, and controlled ablations are needed to support the broad superiority claims.

strengths: The row-wise orthogonal update preserves feasibility exactly and offers potentially inexpensive partial-gradient iterations. With exact subproblem solutions, the majorization construction provides sufficient objective decrease.
Reducing two-row updates to one-dimensional searches over rotations and reflections is a useful algorithmic idea for handling nonsmooth penalties.
Experiments cover ten datasets and three PCA formulations. The nonnegative-PCA results report substantial objective improvements with very small feasibility violations.
weaknesses: The central stationarity hierarchy in Theorem 3.8(a) is false under the stated assumptions. Equations (38)-(39) replace a potentially different subgradient for each block with one common subgradient. A counterexample is h(Y)=||Y||_1, f(Y)=<A,Y>, A=[[-1,-1/2],[-1,1/2],[0,-1]], X=[[q,1/2],[q,-1/2],[0,q]], q=1/sqrt(2), H=Q=0, and α=1. For every two-row block, K(V;X,B)-K(I;X,B)≥||V-I||_F²/4, so X is a global BS2 point. However, min over G∈∂F(X) of ||G-XG^T X||_F² equals 1/4. Thus OBCD can remain at a noncritical fixed point. This also contradicts Lemma 4.4(b) and the claimed convergence to critical points.

The convergence analysis contains an independent sampling error. In Appendix F.2, Equations (51)-(52) exchange the previously selected block with a fresh random block for a matrix depending on the updated iterate X^{t+1}. Because that iterate depends on the previous block, identical sampling marginals do not justify this equality. Appendix F.4 additionally removes random objective differences from conditional expectations without justification. The critical-point complexity and KL convergence-rate claims therefore lack valid proofs.

The main L0-PCA evaluation uses a mathematically trivial parameter regime. Appendix G.2 normalizes ||A||_F=1, giving C=A^T A with tr(C)=1 and 0≤tr(X^T C X)≤1. Every tested λ is at least 10. Consequently, any feasible matrix with more than r nonzeros is worse than an r-sparse coordinate basis, and the global optimum is obtained simply by selecting the r largest diagonal entries of C. This elementary exact baseline is absent, and no meaningful sparsity–variance tradeoff is tested.

The supposedly exact breakpoint solver is incorrect as written. Appendix B gives t=x_i/y_i for x_i+t y_i=0, whereas the correct breakpoint is -x_i/y_i. It also discards coordinates with y_i=0, although their L1 contribution λ|x_i|/sqrt(1+t²) remains dependent on t. These issues require correction and verification because exact subproblem minimization underpins the guarantees.

The remaining comparisons do not isolate algorithmic benefits sufficiently. L1-PCA and nonnegative-PCA experiments use identity initialization for OBCD and random initialization for competitors, confounding optimization method with initialization. Repeated-run uncertainty, adequate baseline-tuning details, and ablations of reflections, block size, and the proximal parameter are missing. Objective traces alone also do not establish the claimed ability to escape local minima.

strengths: The row-wise orthogonal update preserves feasibility and supports inexpensive partial-gradient computations, addressing a relevant class of optimization problems.
The majorization construction provides a useful sufficient-decrease guarantee, and the rotation/reflection parameterization offers a practical approach to two-row subproblems.
Experiments cover three PCA formulations and ten datasets, with several relevant baselines and objective-versus-time comparisons.
weaknesses: The central stationarity hierarchy is false under the stated assumptions. Appendix E.3 requires one subgradient valid simultaneously for all blocks, whereas block optimality only supplies potentially different subgradients. A concrete counterexample uses n=3, r=k=2, h(Y)=||Y||₁, f(Y)=⟨A,Y⟩, Q=0, and α=1. Set a=1/sqrt(2), X=[[0,a],[a,1/2],[a,-1/2]], and A=[[0,a/2−1],[-1,−5/4],[-1,5/4]]. Identity globally minimizes every block surrogate, yet the squared criticality residual defined in the paper equals 1/4. Thus OBCD can remain at a noncritical point, contradicting Theorem 3.8(a), Lemma 4.4(b), and Theorem 4.6. Equation (58) repeats the underlying error by interchanging subgradient minimization and block averaging.

The convergence analysis has additional substantive gaps. Equation (52), step ②, replaces the previous block with a fresh random block even though the updated iterate depends on the previous block; the fixed-matrix averaging identity (51) does not justify this. Appendices F.4–F.5 also turn expectation bounds into pointwise/product bounds without justification and substitute the global infimum F∞ for the limiting objective value. Consequently, the claimed KL and last-iterate guarantees are unsupported.

The main ℓ₀ experiments test an effectively trivial parameter regime. Appendix G.2 normalizes ||A||F=1, so C=AᵀA has trace 1 and explained variance is at most 1, while λ ranges from 10 to 500. Every global optimum therefore has exactly r nonzeros and can be obtained by selecting the r largest diagonal entries of C. This inexpensive exact baseline is omitted, and the experiments do not establish performance on meaningful sparsity–variance tradeoffs.

The claimed exact subproblem solver contains consequential errors as written. Appendix B lists x_i/y_i as a zero of x_i+t y_i instead of −x_i/y_i. It also discards terms with y_i=0, although their ℓ₁ contribution |x_i|/sqrt(1+t²) still depends on t. These require correction and validation because the main guarantees depend on global subproblem solutions. Efficient nonsmooth solving for general k>2 remains assumed rather than demonstrated.

The empirical comparisons do not isolate the proposed algorithm's advantages. For ℓ₁ and nonnegative PCA, OBCD uses identity initialization while competitors use random initialization. Matched initialization experiments, repeated-run uncertainty, and ablations of reflections, exact subproblem minimization, and block size are missing. These limitations weaken the claims of consistently superior optimization and escape from poor local minima.

weaknesses: The central stationarity claim in Theorem 3.8(a) is false under the stated assumptions. Equation (38) permits a different subgradient for each block, whereas Equation (39) requires one subgradient satisfying every block condition simultaneously. A counterexample is f(Y)=⟨A,Y⟩, h(Y)=||Y||₁, A=[[-1,-1],[-1,1],[0,-2]], and X=[[1/√2,1/2],[1/√2,-1/2],[0,1/√2]]. This also contradicts Lemma 4.4(b) and the ε-critical-point guarantee in Theorem 4.6.

The convergence proofs contain additional substantive errors. Equation (52) replaces a fresh sampled block with the previously selected block even though X^{t+1} depends on that previous selection; identical marginal sampling distributions do not justify this equality. Appendix F.4 subsequently uses expectation bounds as pointwise inequalities and removes random objective differences from conditional expectations. Consequently, the claimed KL-based last-iterate guarantees are not established.

Such solutions are signed coordinate vectors, and the optimum follows simply by selecting the r largest diagonal entries of C. This exact baseline is missing, and these experiments do not substantiate effectiveness on challenging sparse PCA problems.

The majorization construction provides a straightforward sufficient-descent argument when subproblems are solved correctly. Reducing two-row updates to one-dimensional searches is practically appealing.
The experiments cover three PCA formulations, ten datasets, and several relevant baseline families, including ManPG, RSSM, and splitting methods.
weaknesses: The central stationarity hierarchy is false as stated. In Theorem 3.8(a), Equation (38) permits different subgradients for different blocks, whereas Equation (39) requires one common subgradient. A counterexample uses X=[(1,1,1)^T/√3, (0,1,−1)^T/√2], g=(2,−1,−1)^T/(2√6), S=[[1,0],[1,1],[1,−1]], and F(Y)=⟨[g,0]−S,Y⟩+||Y||₁. With Q=0 and α=1, every two-row surrogate is globally minimized at I₂, yet the squared full stationarity residual at X is 1/4. Thus global block-2 stationarity need not imply criticality, even with convex separable h. Lemma 4.4(b) contains the corresponding invalid interchange between minimizing over subgradients and averaging over blocks.

The stochastic convergence analysis has additional substantive errors. Appendix F.2, Equations (51)–(52), replaces the updated block Bᵗ with an independent fresh block Bᵗ⁺¹ inside an expression depending on Xᵗ⁺¹, which itself depends on Bᵗ. Identical marginal sampling distributions do not justify this substitution. The KL proof also replaces the limiting objective value with F∞, previously defined as the global infimum, and treats expectation bounds as pointwise bounds. Consequently, the critical-point complexity and last-iterate guarantees are not established.

The exact breakpoint solver is incorrect as described in Appendix B. Zeros of xᵢ+tyᵢ occur at −xᵢ/yᵢ, but the stated L0 candidate set uses +xᵢ/yᵢ. Furthermore, deleting coordinates with yᵢ=0 is invalid for the L1 objective: their contribution λ|xᵢ|/√(1+t²) still depends on t. The main L0-PCA evaluation uses a mathematically degenerate parameter regime. Appendix G.2 normalizes ||A||F=1, so C=AᵀA satisfies tr(C)=1 and 0≤tr(XᵀCX)≤1. Global solutions therefore have exactly r nonzeros and can be obtained by selecting the r largest diagonal entries of C. This elementary exact baseline is absent, and these experiments do not establish performance on meaningful sparsity–variance tradeoffs.

The remaining comparisons do not convincingly isolate algorithmic advantages. For L1-PCA and nonnegative PCA, OBCD uses identity initialization while competitors use random initialization. Reported runtime budgets also disagree: the main text specifies 30 seconds, Table 1 specifies 40, and other results use 60. The advertised scope exceeds the demonstrated guarantees. Efficient global subproblem solution is assumed for general k and h, while concrete nonsmooth solvers address k=2. Moreover, the bounded-subgradient assumption underlying the criticality and KL analyses excludes the L0 penalty and nonnegativity indicator used in two principal applications. strengths: The row-wise orthogonal update preserves feasibility exactly and avoids a full Stiefel retraction. The majorization construction provides a useful sufficient-decrease property.
Reducing two-row subproblems to scalar searches over rotations and reflections is a promising computational approach for separable nonsmooth penalties.
The empirical study covers ten datasets and three PCA formulations, includes recent baselines, and reports runtime curves and nonnegativity violations.
weaknesses: The central optimality claim, Theorem 3.8(a), fails under the stated assumptions. Equations (38)–(39) incorrectly turn block-specific subgradients into one subgradient satisfying every block condition. A counterexample is n=3, r=k=2, q=1/√2, X=[[q,0],[q,0],[0,1]], f(Y)=1.5(Y12−Y22), h(Y)=||Y||_1, H=Q=0, and α=1. Identity globally minimizes every two-row surrogate, making X a BS2 point. Nevertheless, min over G∈∂F(X) of ||G−XGᵀX||_F² equals 1/2, so X is not critical. This also contradicts Lemma 4.4(b) and Theorem 4.6: OBCD initialized at X never moves.

The stochastic convergence proofs contain additional substantive gaps. Equations (51)–(52) apply an expectation identity for a fixed matrix to a matrix depending on the sampled block through X^(t+1). Appendix F.4 then uses expected bounds as pointwise bounds and extracts random factors from expectations without justification. It also substitutes F∞, defined as the global infimum, for the limiting objective value required by the local KL inequality. The claimed last-iterate guarantees are therefore not established.

The exact subproblem solver needs correction. Appendix B lists zeros of xi+t·yi as +xi/yi rather than −xi/yi. It also states that coordinates with yi=0 can be discarded, but for the ℓ1 penalty they contribute λ|xi|/√(1+t²), which is not constant. Since exact global subproblem solutions underpin the guarantees, these issues require corrected derivations and implementation validation.

The main ℓ0 experiments use a degenerate regularization regime. Appendix G.2 normalizes ||A||_F=1, implying C is positive semidefinite with trace 1 and 0≤tr(XᵀCX)≤1. Every tested λ is at least 10. Thus, for the stated ℓ0 objective, any additional nonzero costs more than the entire possible variance improvement. A global optimum consists of exactly r signed coordinate vectors corresponding to the r largest diagonal entries of C. This simple exact baseline is missing, and these experiments do not demonstrate performance on challenging sparse PCA instances.

The comparisons do not adequately isolate algorithmic improvements. For ℓ1 SPCA, OBCD receives identity initialization while every competitor receives random initialization. Matched-start comparisons, repeated-run uncertainty, baseline tuning details, and ablations of reflections and the proximal parameter are missing. Short runtime curves without stationarity checks also do not establish the claim that competing methods remain trapped in poor local minima.

strengths: The problem is relevant to sparse and nonnegative representation learning. Row-wise orthogonal updates naturally accommodate rectangular Stiefel matrices while preserving feasibility.
The majorization and proximal construction provides a useful sufficient-descent property, with potentially inexpensive partial-gradient updates.

The rotation/reflection parameterization for k=2 is constructive. The manuscript includes extensive derivations and comparisons against several relevant baselines across ten datasets, with substantial reported improvements on nonnegative PCA.
weaknesses: The central stationarity hierarchy, Theorem 3.8(a), is false under the stated assumptions. Consider a=1/sqrt(2), X0=[[0,1],[a,0],[a,0]], h(X)=||X||1, and f(X)=-X12-X21-X31-1.5X22+1.5X32. Every two-row orthogonal update has F(X)>=F(X0)=0. Consequently, with H=Q=0, X0 is a BS2 point for every positive proximal parameter. However, X(t)=[[0,cos(t)],[a,a sin(t)],[a,-a sin(t)]] remains feasible and satisfies F(X(t))=-a sin(t) for small positive t. Thus X0 has a negative feasible directional derivative and is not critical. Appendix E.3 makes the corresponding quantifier error: block optimality supplies a potentially different subgradient for each block, whereas Equation (39) requires one subgradient satisfying every block condition simultaneously.

The same counterexample invalidates Lemma 4.4(b) and the general critical-point guarantee in Theorem 4.6: every proximal block update uniquely selects the identity, so OBCD remains at the noncritical X0 indefinitely. There are additional problems in the stochastic proofs. Equations (51)-(52) apply a fixed-matrix sampling identity to a matrix depending on the previously selected block through X^(t+1). Appendix F.4 then uses expectation bounds as pathwise inequalities and removes random factors from expectations without justification. The claimed convergence guarantees therefore require substantial revision.

The main ℓ0 experiments evaluate a regime with a simple exact solution. Appendix G.2 normalizes ||A||F=1, giving C=A^T A positive semidefinite with trace(C)=1 and 0<=trace(X^T C X)<=1. Every tested penalty satisfies lambda>=10. A feasible matrix with more than r nonzeros consequently has objective at least lambda(r+1)-1>lambda r, while coordinate columns achieve at most lambda r. The global optimum therefore has exactly r nonzeros and is obtained by selecting the r largest diagonal entries of C. This exact sorting baseline is missing, and the experiments do not establish performance in a nontrivial variance-sparsity tradeoff.

The ℓ1 comparisons confound the algorithm with initialization: all competing methods start randomly, while OBCD starts from an identity matrix, which already attains the minimum possible ℓ1 penalty on the Stiefel manifold. Matched initialization experiments, variability across random seeds, and a documented baseline-tuning protocol are needed. The manuscript also inconsistently specifies 30 seconds in the experimental description versus 40 seconds in Table 1.

The practical evidence is narrower than the general framework suggests. Efficient global subproblem solution is developed primarily for k=2; general nonsmooth larger-block guarantees depend on an exact optimization oracle whose tractability is explicitly unresolved. There are no convincing ablations isolating block size, reflections, or the surrogate-curvature choice.

strengths: The row-wise orthogonal update preserves Stiefel feasibility exactly and permits inexpensive partial-gradient updates.
The reduction to rotations and reflections for k=2 is useful for nonsmooth objectives. The majorization construction provides a valid sufficient-descent argument under exact subproblem minimization.
Experiments cover three PCA formulations across ten datasets, include relevant methods such as ManPG, RADMM, and RSSM, and report promising nonnegative-PCA results.
weaknesses: The central optimality claim, Theorem 3.8(a), is false as stated. Equation (38) provides a potentially different subgradient for each block, whereas Equation (39) requires one common subgradient. A counterexample is f(Y)=⟨A,Y⟩, h(Y)=||Y||_1, H=Q=0, α=1, with a=1/√2, X=[[a,0],[1/2,a],[1/2,-a]], and A=[[-1,0],[-1/2,-1],[-1/2,1]]. For every two-row block, K(V;X,B)-K(I;X,B)≥||V-I||_F²/4, so X is a global block-2 stationary point. Nevertheless, its criticality residual dist(0,∂_M F(X)) equals 1/2. This also contradicts Lemma 4.4(b) and the claimed convergence to critical points.

The stochastic convergence proof has an additional independence error. Equations (51)–(52) interchange the previously selected block and a fresh block for a matrix depending on X^{t+1}, although X^{t+1} depends on the previous selection. Equal sampling distributions do not justify this substitution. Appendix F.4 subsequently uses expectation bounds as pathwise inequalities. Consequently, the stated KL convergence rates are not established.

The exact subproblem solver contains consequential errors. Appendix B discards terms with y_i=0, although their ℓ1 contribution λ|x_i|/√(1+t²) depends on t. It also lists x_i/y_i rather than -x_i/y_i as zeros of x_i+t y_i. These issues require correction and solver validation because exact global minimization underpins the guarantees.

The main ℓ0-PCA benchmark is degenerate under the stated settings. Appendix G.2 normalizes ||A||_F=1, implying tr(C)=1 and 0≤tr(XᵀCX)≤1. With every tested λ≥10, an optimum must have exactly r nonzeros; selecting the r largest diagonal entries of C solves the problem globally. This elementary baseline is absent, and the experiments therefore do not establish performance on nontrivial sparsity–variance tradeoffs.

Experimental comparisons do not adequately isolate the algorithmic contribution. OBCD uses identity initialization while the ℓ1-PCA and nonnegative-PCA baselines use random initialization. Matched-start comparisons, variability across random trials, and ablations of reflections and exact block minimization are missing. Baseline tuning is insufficiently documented, and the stated 30-second budget conflicts with Table 1's 40-second budget.

Please serve as an expert reviewer for a top-tier AI conference with an acceptance rate of about 30%.
Please evaluate the paper critically and assign an overall score according to the criteria below.

Assign an Overall Assessment (OA) score according to the rating scale below.
Choose an OA score from: 1, 3, 5, 6, 8, or 10.

Rating scale:
1 = Strong Reject
A paper with fundamental problems such as well-known or trivial results, serious technical flaws, unsupported central claims, invalid evaluation, or unaddressed ethical concerns.

3 = Reject
A paper that is not competitive for a top-tier AI conference due to meaningful weaknesses in novelty, technical soundness, evaluation, reproducibility, clarity, significance, or positioning.
A paper can receive 3 even if it is understandable, technically plausible, or has some strengths, if the overall contribution or evidence is insufficient.

5 = Marginally below the acceptance threshold
A technically solid paper with some positive qualities, but where the reasons for a lower score slightly outweigh the reasons for a higher score.
Typical reasons include limited novelty, incomplete evaluation, weak or missing baselines, insufficient ablations, unclear significance, narrow scope, limited reproducibility, or claims that are stronger than the evidence.
Please use sparingly.

6 = Marginally above the acceptance threshold
A technically solid paper where the reasons for a higher score clearly outweigh the weaknesses.
A rating of 6 requires concrete positive evidence that the paper is competitive for a top-tier AI conference, such as a clear contribution, convincing evaluation, appropriate baselines, and sufficient support for the main claims.
Do not assign 6 merely because the paper is coherent, plausible, or has some positive results.
Please use sparingly.

8 = Accept
A strong paper with a clear and meaningful contribution, convincing technical quality, good-to-excellent evaluation, appropriate comparisons, sufficient reproducibility, and clear relevance to the field.
The paper should have high impact on at least one sub-area of AI or moderate-to-high impact on more than one area of AI.
Minor weaknesses are acceptable, but there should be no major unresolved issues in soundness, evaluation, novelty, or ethics.

10 = Strong Accept
An exceptional paper with groundbreaking impact on one or more areas of AI, technically excellent work, exceptionally strong evaluation, strong reproducibility and resources, and no unaddressed ethical considerations.
This rating should be reserved for rare submissions that are clearly among the best papers in the venue.

Output Format

Provide your review in JSON format. Use a numeric value for oa and lists of text for strengths and weaknesses:

{"oa": <num>, "strengths": ["<text>"], "weaknesses": ["<text>"]}

q=1/np.sqrt(2)
X=np.array([[0,q,q],[q,.5,-.5],[q,-.5,.5]])
A=q/2*np.array([[0,1,-1],[-1,0,0],[1,0,0]])

print('Full squared stationarity residual at optimal z=0:',np.linalg.norm((M+S)-X@(M+S).T@X)**2)

def plus(A,B,scale=1):return [[x+scale*y for x,y in zip(a,b)] for a,b in zip(A,B)]
def norm2(A):return sum(x*x for row in A for x in row)
def dot(A,B):return sum(x*y for a,b in zip(A,B) for x,y in zip(a,b))
def block(A,B):return [[A[i][j] for j in B] for i in B]
X=[[0,q,q],[q,.5,-.5],[q,-.5,.5]]
A=[[0,q/2,-q/2],[-q/2,0,0],[q/2,0,0]]
S=[[0 if x==0 else (1 if x>0 else -1) for x in row] for row in X]
D=[[.5*x for x in row] for row in mm(A,X)]
M=plus(D,S,-1)
I=[[1,0,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,1]]

    print('Block',[i+1 for i in B],'z',z,'skew error',norm2(plus(W,tr(W),-1)),'lambda_max',abs(W[0][1]))
    Z=[X[i] for i in B]

strengths: Small orthogonal row updates preserve feasibility exactly and can exploit partial gradients, offering a computationally attractive alternative to full retractions.
Combining rotations and reflections with one-dimensional subproblems is useful. The basic sufficient-decrease argument is sound under exact surrogate minimization.
The experiments cover three relevant applications and ten datasets, with comparisons including ManPG, RADMM, and RSSM.
weaknesses: The central stationarity hierarchy is false under the stated assumptions. Appendix E.3 incorrectly replaces a potentially different subgradient for each block with one common subgradient; Lemma 4.4(b) repeats this problem. An explicit counterexample is q=1/sqrt(2), X=[[0,q,q],[q,1/2,-1/2],[q,-1/2,1/2]], W=(q/2)[[0,1,-1],[-1,0,0],[1,0,0]], and f(Y)=<WX/2-S,Y>, where S is the entrywise sign of X with S11=0. Set h(Y)=||Y||1, Q=0, and alpha=1. Every two-row surrogate is globally minimized at identity, yet the minimum squared criticality residual ||G-XG^T X||_F^2 over G in ∂F(X) equals 1/2. Thus OBCD can remain at a BS2 point that is not critical, contradicting Theorem 3.8(a) and the claimed general criticality guarantee.

The convergence analysis has additional substantive errors. Equations (51)–(52) exchange the previously selected block with a fresh independent block even though X^{t+1} depends on the previous block. Appendix F.4 then uses expectation bounds as pointwise bounds and removes a random objective difference from an expectation. It also substitutes F∞, defined as the global infimum, for the limiting objective without establishing global optimality. Consequently, the claimed criticality complexity and KL convergence rates are not established.

The exact subproblem solver is incorrect as written. Appendix B lists x_i/y_i as a breakpoint for x_i+t y_i=0, whose solution is -x_i/y_i. It also permits dropping coordinates with y_i=0, although their L1 contribution lambda|x_i|/sqrt(1+t^2) generally depends on t. These errors undermine the exact-minimization assumption on which the guarantees depend.

The main L0 experiments evaluate a degenerate regularization regime. Appendix G.2 normalizes ||A||_F=1, implying trace(C)=1 and 0≤trace(X^T C X)≤1. With every tested lambda≥10, adding even one nonzero beyond the minimum r costs more than any possible variance improvement. Global optimization therefore reduces to choosing the r coordinate axes with largest C_ii. This elementary exact baseline is missing, and the results do not establish performance on a meaningful sparsity–variance tradeoff.

Experimental controls are insufficient to attribute improvements to the algorithm. For L1 sparse PCA and nonnegative PCA, OBCD receives identity initialization while competitors receive random initialization, a substantial confound in these nonconvex problems. Repeated-run uncertainty and baseline tuning details are missing, and Section 5 specifies a 30-second budget while Table 1 specifies 40 seconds. Finite-duration convergence plots also cannot substantiate the assertion that competitors remain trapped regardless of runtime.

The demonstrated scope is narrower than the advertised framework. Efficient global nonsmooth subproblem solution is developed only for k=2; the general-k result assumes the difficult solver, while the local-solution fallback loses the strongest claimed guarantee. The bounded-subgradient assumption needed for the later convergence results excludes the central L0 and nonnegativity-indicator examples. 1 = Strong Reject
A paper with fundamental problems such as well-known or trivial results, serious technical flaws, unsupported central claims, invalid evaluation, or unaddressed ethical concerns.

3 = Reject
A paper that is not competitive for a top-tier AI conference due to meaningful weaknesses in novelty, technical soundness, evaluation, reproducibility, clarity, significance, or positioning.
A paper can receive 3 even if it is understandable, technically plausible, or has some strengths, if the overall contribution or evidence is insufficient.

5 = Marginally below the acceptance threshold
A technically solid paper with some positive qualities, but where the reasons for a lower score slightly outweigh the reasons for a higher score.
Typical reasons include limited novelty, incomplete evaluation, weak or missing baselines, insufficient ablations, unclear significance, narrow scope, limited reproducibility, or claims that are stronger than the evidence.
Please use sparingly.

6 = Marginally above the acceptance threshold
A technically solid paper where the reasons for a higher score clearly outweigh the weaknesses.
A rating of 6 requires concrete positive evidence that the paper is competitive for a top-tier AI conference, such as a clear contribution, convincing evaluation, appropriate baselines, and sufficient support for the main claims.
Do not assign 6 merely because the paper is coherent, plausible, or has some positive results.
Please use sparingly.

8 = Accept
A strong paper with a clear and meaningful contribution, convincing technical quality, good-to-excellent evaluation, appropriate comparisons, sufficient reproducibility, and clear relevance to the field.
The paper should have high impact on at least one sub-area of AI or moderate-to-high impact on more than one area of AI.
Minor weaknesses are acceptable, but there should be no major unresolved issues in soundness, evaluation, novelty, or ethics.

10 = Strong Accept
An exceptional paper with groundbreaking impact on one or more areas of AI, technically excellent work, exceptionally strong evaluation, strong reproducibility and resources, and no unaddressed ethical considerations.
This rating should be reserved for rare submissions that are clearly among the best papers in the venue.

strengths: The orthogonal row-update mechanism preserves feasibility and offers inexpensive partial-gradient iterations. The sufficient-decrease argument is sound when the surrogate subproblems are solved exactly.
Including both rotations and reflections provides a useful parameterization of the two-row subproblem for nonsmooth optimization.
Experiments cover ten datasets and three PCA formulations, include relevant baselines such as ManPG and RADMM, and report nonnegativity violations.
weaknesses: The central stationarity hierarchy is false under the stated assumptions. Consider n=3, r=k=2, h(X)=||X||_1, f(X)=<D,X>, D=[[-1,-1],[-1,1],[1.5,0]], and X0=[[1,1],[1,-1],[0,0]]/sqrt(2). Every two-row orthogonal update has F(X)>=F(X0)=0. Thus, with H=Q=0 and any positive proximal parameter, X0 is a BS2 point and OBCD remains there. However, every ambient subgradient has zero first two rows and third row (1.5+u,v), with u,v in [-1,1], giving a minimum Riemannian stationarity residual of 0.5. This contradicts Theorem 3.8(a), Lemma 4.4(b), and Theorem 4.6. Equations (38)-(39) incorrectly infer a common subgradient satisfying every block condition from the existence of potentially different subgradients for individual blocks.

The convergence analysis has additional independent gaps. In Appendix F.2, Equation (52) exchanges the selected block B_t with a fresh block B_{t+1}, although the matrix being restricted depends on X^{t+1} and therefore on B_t. The sampling identity does not justify this exchange. Appendix F.4 subsequently treats expectation bounds as pathwise inequalities and removes random factors from expectations. The claimed KL convergence rates require a substantially revised argument.

The exact subproblem solver contains correctness errors as written. Appendix B lists x_i/y_i as the zero of x_i+t*y_i, whereas the zero is -x_i/y_i. It also discards coordinates with y_i=0; for the L1 objective, these contribute lambda*|x_i|/sqrt(1+t^2), which can change the minimizer. These issues need correction and solver verification because exact minimization supports the main guarantees.

The entire L0 experimental regime has a simple exact solution that is omitted as a baseline. Appendix G.2 normalizes ||A||_F=1, so C=A^T A has trace one and 0<=tr(X^T C X)<=1. With every tested lambda>=10, any global optimizer must have exactly r nonzeros: an additional nonzero costs more than the maximum possible variance gain. Consequently, selecting the r largest diagonal entries of C gives a global solution using signed coordinate vectors. These experiments do not establish effectiveness on challenging sparse-PCA instances; meaningful regularization regimes and the exact selection baseline are needed.

The remaining comparisons do not adequately isolate the algorithm's advantage. For L1 SPCA, OBCD uses sparse identity initialization while every competitor uses random initialization, a consequential difference under the very large regularization weights. Repeated-run uncertainty, matched-initialization comparisons, and ablations of reflections and the proximal parameter are absent. The reported objective improvements therefore provide insufficient support for the broad claims about escaping poor local minima.
